consumedBy.note: Each `descriptor` is exactly an AssessmentItemDescriptor and carries no other key. Authoring evidence lives beside it under `authoring`, which no runtime reads. There is no answer key in this file and verify.mjs fails if a key-shaped field appears — see answer-key.json.

idiom.options: Four options, A–D, one unambiguously correct. STAAR alternates A–D and F–J by item position; position is a property of a form rather than of an item, so authored items use A–D and the two released items keep TEA's own letters.
idiom.distractors: Every distractor is a real misconception rather than filler. Each one is named in `authoring.distractors` with the misunderstanding it catches, so a wrong answer tells a teacher something.
idiom.reading: Stems are written at the same bar as the module: a thirteen-year-old reads them without a dictionary, and no option is longer than the stem.

provenance.note: Cause-and-effect diagram with a missing middle step, which is a standard STAAR Grade 8 Social Studies stimulus form.

descriptor.stem:
Britain's war with France ends (1763)  →  ?  →  Parliament passes the Stamp Act (1765)

Which event best completes this diagram?

options.text: Colonial assemblies ask Parliament to raise money on their behalf.
Britain is left owing a large debt and looks to the colonies for money to help pay it.
Britain ends all trade between itself and the colonies.
The colonies begin printing their own money to pay for the war.

authoring.askedBy: the middle of the causal chain, supplied by the student
authoring.distinctFrom: The released RECALL item asks the motive as a label. This asks the student to supply the step that connects two dates, which a student can fail while still recognising the motive.

distractors.A: The colonies asked for it — the circular misreading Mission-Slate §4.9 rejects in the duel bank's WHY_NOW.
distractors.C: Trade was cut off — confuses revenue policy with the later non-importation and port closure.
distractors.D: The colonies paid for the war themselves — a plausible reading of 'the colonies paid' that gets the direction backwards.

descriptor.stem: After the war with France, Britain owed more money than it had ever owed before. Parliament decided that part of the money to pay that debt should come from —

options.text: landowners in Britain, who had gained the most from the war
France, as the defeated power
the American colonies
loans from other European governments

authoring.askedBy: the edge of who the policy points at
authoring.distinctFrom: ORDERING asks what happened between two dates; this asks who the resulting policy reached for. A student can hold the chain and still think Britain taxed itself.

distractors.A: Britain taxed itself — the answer a student gives who has the debt but not the colonial half.
distractors.B: The loser pays — reasonable-sounding, and the wrong century's idea of a war settlement.
distractors.D: Borrow more — plausible and the thing the debt already was.

provenance.note: The proposition is stated in TEA's own 2023 constructed-response scoring guide as the rubric bullet 'All colonists had to pay taxes on documents and paper.' No released selectable item tests it.

descriptor.stem: The Stamp Act of 1765 required colonists to buy a paid stamp for —

options.text: all goods unloaded at colonial ports
food and cloth sold in colonial markets
tools and ironwork made by colonial blacksmiths
printed and legal papers, such as newspapers and court documents

authoring.distinctFrom: BOUNDARY asks the student to exclude; this asks them to include. A student running a 'the British taxed everything' heuristic can pass neither, but a student who has only half the boundary passes one.

distractors.A: Imports — the Sugar Act's shape, and the boundary an eighth grader who has met one customs duty reaches for first.
distractors.B: Everyday purchases — the apprentice's error, in option form.
distractors.C: Manufactured goods — the misreading that the Act attacked colonial industry.

descriptor.stem: From 1 November 1765, which of these would NOT have needed a paid stamp?

options.text: A newspaper printed in Boston
A deed recorded in a colonial court
A barrel of nails sold at a shop
A licence issued to a tavern keeper

authoring.distinctFrom: RECALL names the category and this one hides it. Three of the four options are inside the Act, so a student who has memorised 'paper is taxed' without the boundary now has three answers that look right and must find the one that is not paper at all. This is the pairing the shrinking retry needs: passing RECALL and failing BOUNDARY is a real and diagnosable state.

distractors.A: Inside — the printed half, and the most memorable example.
distractors.D: Inside — a licence is the example a student is least likely to have met, so choosing it is the tell for a shallow list rather than a category.

authoring.negativeStemNote: STAAR does use NOT-stems and capitalises the word, which is why it is capitalised here. It is the only negative stem in the pool; two would be a reading trap rather than a measurement.

descriptor.stem: Parliament passed the Stamp Act in March 1765. In August 1765, Boston's printers were still printing on unstamped paper. Which statement best explains this?

options.text: The Act's stamp duties did not take effect until 1 November 1765.
Parliament repealed the Act a few months after passing it.
The Act applied only to colonies south of New England.
Printers had been given a permanent exemption from the Act.

authoring.askedBy: the gap between passage and effect
authoring.distinctFrom: Neither scope item touches time. This one hands the student the March date and asks what accounts for the delay, so the November date does work rather than being recited.

distractors.B: Repeal — true in 1766 and not in 1765, which makes it the strongest distractor for a student who knows a little more than the module taught.
distractors.C: Regional scope — invented, and catches a student guessing at any explanation.
distractors.D: Printers exempt — the opposite of the concept, and the tell for a student who has absorbed that printers were the loudest opponents without knowing why.

authoring.answerabilityNote: The stem supplies March, so the student needs only 1 November, which the module's stamp card states outright.

descriptor.stem: Which statement describes the people of Boston and their representation in 1765?

options.text: They elected members to Parliament but had no colonial assembly of their own.
They elected members to their own colonial assembly but no members to Parliament.
They elected members to both Parliament and their own colonial assembly.
They elected no representatives to any governing body.

authoring.askedBy: the fact the whole argument rests on
authoring.distinctFrom: The released DISCRIMINATION item asks why a resolution was adopted; this asks the plain fact underneath it. A student can pick the right reason from a quotation and still not know that Boston elected anything at all.

distractors.A: The reverse — a student who has heard 'no representation' and applied it to the wrong body.
distractors.D: Nothing — the over-reading of 'no representation' into 'no self-government', which is the misconception that makes the whole objection incoherent.

descriptor.stem: On the colonists' own argument, a tax laid on them would have been lawful only if it had been voted by —

options.text: Parliament, because it governed the whole British Empire
The royal governor, who was appointed by the King
No body at all, because the colonists held that taxation itself was unlawful
The Massachusetts assembly, whose members the colonists elected

authoring.askedBy: the line between an authority the colonists accepted and one they did not
authoring.distinctFrom: RECALL asks what Boston elected; this asks what follows from it. The concept is a claim about legitimate authority, and this is the only item in the pool that asks the student to point at the legitimate one rather than at the illegitimate one.

distractors.A: The Crown's own answer, stated fairly. A student who has absorbed 'Parliament ruled the empire' without the consent argument picks it.
distractors.B: The governor — appointed rather than elected, which is the same error the concept exists to catch, moved one office over.
distractors.C: The over-claim. Mission-Slate §4.9 rejects it in the duel bank and it belongs here as a distractor, because it is what a student reaches for who thinks the objection was to paying rather than to who asked.
